 New to Wh, surge or UPS switchover? Our power station glossary explains each spec in one place.
 For charging, we compare only 0 to 100% times from a wall outlet. A model that lists only 0 to 80% does not rank on this rule. A fast mode you turn on in the app counts and is named on the card.
 These rules find the leader on one stated number. They do not show that a model is the best choice for every appliance, installation or way of charging. The "Closest alternative" and "Skip it if" lines cover that.
 Prices. We check the brand's US store each day for the price of the base working configuration, without solar panels or optional extra batteries. A discount the store shows on the product page counts and is marked "with coupon". Our affiliate codes are shown beside the offer and do not count in the price or the ranking. A price older than 72 hours does not rank. Rankings use the unrounded price per watt-hour, and the page shows it rounded to two decimals.
 Independent tests. A test counts if it covers the version sold in the US (named as the US model, or a unit bought and tested in the US), has a date and explains what was measured. We leave out other regional versions and results we cannot reconcile with the stated method or capacity. Tests add context to the specs and can flag a problem. They do not pick the winner, because most models have no comparable test. If a test calls a pick into question, we review it.
 What these picks do not tell you. We have not run these stations ourselves. Runtimes are our calculations, not appliance tests. A pick can change when a verified price, stock status, spec or test changes. The full method is on How we rate .
 What to look for in a portable power station
 Wh Capacity: how long A 1,024Wh station runs a 100W TV for about 8.7 hours.
 W Output: what runs at once Add up everything that is on at the same time.
 Surge W Start-up: motors A fridge or a pump needs a short peak to start.
 Capacity (Wh) is how long. Multiply each device’s average watts by its hours, add them up, add our 20% allowance (× 1.2) and divide by 0.85. That is the rated capacity to look for. Our size calculator does it for your list.
 Output (W) is what runs at once. A “1kWh class” unit does not mean 1,000W of output. Add up everything that runs together.
 Surge is for motors. Fridges, pumps and air conditioners draw several times their running watts for a moment at start-up. A rating on paper is not a guarantee, so test the exact appliance before an outage. Some stations list a mode that runs heaters above their rated output by lowering the voltage. That does not raise the rating for motors.
 Weight decides where it goes. Think about how far and how often you will move it. Compare the weight of the complete working system and of its heaviest piece. Modular systems move in separate pieces, and large all-in-one stations need wheels or a second person.
 Illustration made with Adobe Firefly from EcoFlow product photos. 
 Charging: the wall recharge time matters when outages repeat. For solar, check three limits on the input: watts, voltage and current. With our 75% panel figure, 1,000Wh from a 400W array takes about 3.3 equivalent full-sun hours, before charging losses. That is not 3.3 hours on the clock.
 Extra batteries: count the full system price and check that the battery is in stock. 18 of the 31 models support compatible extra batteries. An extra battery adds stored energy. It does not raise the output rating of the inverter or add 240V.
 House circuits: a station feeds circuits in your panel only through a transfer switch or an inlet with a panel interlock, installed by a licensed electrician. Never plug it into a wall outlet to feed the house.
 When a portable power station is the wrong choice
 Central air or the whole house at once. Most homes need an installed standby generator or a home battery system for that.
 Long outages with no way to recharge. Without sun or a generator, any station runs out. A gas generator that runs a few hours a day can recharge it.
 Lowering your power bill. Charging from the grid and using that energy later does not save money unless your utility charges less at night, and the battery wears with every cycle.
 Heating. A 1,500W heater empties a 2kWh station in about 1.2 hours.
 Which brand makes the best portable power stations?
 No brand leads every size group in our data. EcoFlow and Jackery have a model in all five groups, Anker SOLIX and BLUETTI in the three middle groups. Warranty terms, support records and recalls differ, and our brand comparison lists them for all four.
 How to check safety certification
 Check the certification of the exact model, not a mention of a standard in an ad. UL 2743 is the safety standard for portable power packs. Confirm the listing with the organization that issued it: UL Product iQ covers listings by UL Solutions, and other certifiers keep their own directories. A portable listing does not make a station a certified home battery system. A battery installed as part of the home needs the complete system listed to UL 9540, according to IAEI Magazine .
 Battery chemistry and rated lifespan
 Every model we track but one uses LiFePO4 (lithium iron phosphate) cells. The exception, the BLUETTI Pioneer Na , uses sodium-ion cells. Makers rate LiFePO4 stations for 3,000 to 6,000 cycles to 70 or 80% of the original capacity. Older NMC stations are rated far lower: the first Jackery Explorer 1000 lists 500 cycles to 80%. A cycle rating is a rated endurance figure, not a forecast of service life. Batteries also age with time, and a station at 70 or 80% still works with less runtime. More in our guide to how long a power station lasts .
 Questions buyers ask
 What is the best portable power station? It depends on what you need to run and for how long. Under our rules, the EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus is the compact pick, the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 charges fastest at 1kWh, the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 costs least per watt-hour among the 2kWh models in stock, the Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus does the same with 240V, and the EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra X has the most capacity with extra batteries.
 What size portable power station do I need? Add up the average watts of what you want to run and the hours you need, then add our 20% allowance. For phones and a laptop, a small unit is enough. For a fridge overnight, start at 2kWh. The size calculator checks your list against every model we track.
 How do you charge a portable power station? From a wall outlet, solar panels, a car 12V socket or a generator through the AC input. The wall is the fastest on most models. Solar depends on the panels, the sun and the input limits of the station. A car socket is often limited to about 10A at 12V, so car charging is slow. Check the station's supported car input and cable before estimating the time.
 Can a portable power station run a refrigerator? Yes, if its output covers the fridge's start and its capacity covers the hours. By our calculation, a full-size fridge that averages 100W runs for about 17 hours on 2kWh and about 8.7 hours on 1,024Wh.
 Can a portable power station power a house? A suitable system can supply selected circuits through a transfer switch or an inlet with an interlock, installed by a licensed electrician. Whether it runs a fridge, a furnace blower or a well pump depends on voltage, what runs at the same time, start-up surge and the installation. Capacity alone does not settle it. Our guide on whether a power station can run a house works through the numbers.
 Is a portable power station the same as a solar generator? The terms often mean the same device: a battery, an inverter and a charge controller in one case. "Solar generator" usually describes a station sold with solar panels. Our solar generator kits page compares kit prices with the parts bought separately.
 Can I leave a portable power station plugged in? Many can stay plugged in and switch to battery when the grid drops, but it depends on the model and its mode, so follow its manual. Published switchover times, 0 to 30 ms among the models we track, apply to specific modes and outlets, so they are not interchangeable. Some brands ask for a full cycle every few months during storage, and some warranties require it.
 How long do portable power stations last? LiFePO4 models are rated for 3,000 to 6,000 cycles. At one full cycle a day, 3,000 cycles is about 8 years. With occasional use, age wears the battery before the cycles do.

 Portable power stations used to be camping gear for people who already owned solar panels. Now they’re closer to home infrastructure. That’s not curiosity traffic. Those are buyers trying to keep routers, refrigerators, laptops, CPAP machines, and weekend gear running without dragging a gas generator out of the garage.
 The mistake is buying by watt-hours alone. A 288Wh box can be the right answer for a router and laptop. A 2,000Wh station can be the right answer for a refrigerator and sump pump. A cheap station with weak AC output can be worse than a smaller one that charges faster and uses safer LFP cells.

 How to choose without wasting money
 Capacity tells you how long the station can run a load. Output tells you what it can start and keep running. Those are different buying decisions. A router and modem may draw 20 to 40W combined. A full-size refrigerator can spike much higher at startup, even if its running draw looks harmless. That’s why a small station can be great for internet backup and useless for a kitchen outage.
 Battery chemistry matters too. For anything you plan to keep for years, LFP is the baseline I’d buy now. The models here use LFP or are sold as LiFePO4 units, which generally means better cycle life and safer long-term storage than the older lithium-ion stations that filled the category a few years ago.
 Charging speed is the last thing buyers underrate. If the grid comes back for two hours, a station that refills fast is more useful than a larger one that crawls. That’s especially true during rolling outages, road trips, and solar-charging windows where sun moves quickly.

 Price : $219
 Where to Buy : Amazon 
 The BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 is the small station I’d buy before a normal UPS if the goal is more runtime and more flexibility. The useful part is a 288Wh LFP battery, 600W continuous AC output, 1500W power lifting, two USB-C ports rated up to 140W and 100W, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth app control, and a 10ms UPS mode. At 9.4 pounds, it’s still a grab-and-go box.
 That spec mix makes sense for modern home problems. A modem, router, mini PC, laptop, camera battery charger, or CPAP backup doesn’t need a 50-pound battery. It needs enough clean power to ride through an outage and enough USB-C output to avoid charger clutter.
 The limit is capacity. A 288Wh battery isn’t a refrigerator plan. It’s the station for keeping communications alive, finishing work during a blackout, powering a diesel heater, or running lights at a campsite. Buy the Elite 30 V2 when portability matters more than appliance runtime.
 BLUETTI AC70 Portable Power Station 
 Price : $328.99
 Where to Buy : Amazon 
 The BLUETTI AC70 is the first step up from gadget backup into real weekend power. The live listing shows 768Wh of capacity, 1000W AC output, 2000W power lifting, 500W solar input, 950W max AC charging, two AC outlets, and a 22.5-pound weight. That’s a practical middle size for camping, a work shed, camera gear, a router plus computer setup, or small appliances that don’t need all-day runtime.
 I like this size because it forces realistic expectations. It can run more than laptops and phones, but it’s still small enough to move without planning your whole garage around it. The AC70 is also a good fit if you want to learn solar charging before buying a full 2kWh station.
 Read the runtime math before you plug in a heater or coffee maker. A customer review on the listing points out that usable AC energy can land lower than the 768Wh headline after inverter losses and self-consumption. That’s not a BLUETTI-only issue. It’s how these stations work. Buy it for moderate loads, not for running high-wattage heat all night.
 Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 Portable Power Station 
 Price : $448.99
 Where to Buy : Amazon 
 The Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 is the easiest recommendation for someone who asks, “Which one should I buy if I don’t want to overthink this?” The useful part is a 1070Wh LiFePO4 battery, 1500W AC output, 3000W surge, 100W USB-C, one-hour fast charging, and a 23.8-pound weight.
 That combination is why this sits in the center of the guide. It’s large enough for a mini fridge, laptop station, lights, Starlink-style internet gear, camera charging, and typical camping electronics. It’s not so large that it becomes garage equipment.
 The Jackery interface is also less intimidating than some app-heavy stations. For emergency gear, that is the useful part. If the power goes out and someone else in the house needs to use it, the buttons and display need to make sense without a manual.
 The trade is price competition. BLUETTI and EcoFlow often undercut Jackery on watts per dollar. Jackery still earns the default spot because weight, reputation, and the 1kWh capacity line up cleanly. If I were buying one station for general household and car-camping use, this would be one of the first listings I’d check.
 EcoFlow DELTA 2 Portable Power Station 
 Price : $449
 Where to Buy : Amazon 
 The EcoFlow DELTA 2 is the pick for buyers who care about recharge speed and expansion. The useful part is 1024Wh of LFP capacity, 1800W AC output, a large port array, and fast AC charging.
 EcoFlow’s advantage is the system around the box. If you want app controls, expansion batteries, and a path toward a larger home-backup setup, the DELTA 2 is easier to justify than a simpler one-piece station. It’s also strong for apartment backup because you can keep it inside, charge it fast from the wall, and avoid fuel, exhaust, and storage issues.
 The caution is complexity. More app control and expansion options also mean more settings, firmware, fan behavior, and ecosystem decisions. If you want a station that sits on a shelf until a storm, the Jackery may feel calmer. If you want to grow the setup later, EcoFlow has the better runway.
 BLUETTI AC180 Portable Power Station 
 Price : $599
 Where to Buy : Amazon 
 The BLUETTI AC180 is the value play when you need more muscle than the AC70 but don’t want to cross into 2kWh pricing. The useful part is 1152Wh of LFP capacity, 1800W AC output, 2700W peak output, 8 outlets, and 0 to 80 percent charging in about 45 minutes. At $599, it sits in a useful gap.
 That gap is appliance territory. A station around this size can cover short refrigerator runs, a microwave burst, a coffee maker, tools, or a heavier camping setup better than the small boxes can. It’s also strong as a backup for people who want one station that can handle normal electronics and a few higher-wattage tasks.
 The cost is weight. At 35.3 pounds, the AC180 is portable in the same way a full cooler is portable. You can move it, but you won’t want to carry it across a campsite five times a day. Buy this for home, RV, shed, or car-adjacent use.
 Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 Portable Power Station 
 Price : $599
 Where to Buy : Amazon 
 The Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 is for the buyer who values fast turnaround more than the lowest shelf price. The useful part is a 1024Wh LiFePO4 battery, 2000W rated output, 3000W peak output, a 49-minute full charge claim, and 10 outlets.
 That 49-minute charging claim is the hook. If you’re dealing with unreliable power, short generator windows, or a road trip where wall time is scarce, fast refill speed changes how often the station is useful. You can top it off during a lunch stop or between outage windows instead of waiting half a day.
 Anker also has a strong accessory and charger reputation, which matters when the station is part of a larger pile of USB-C gear. A power station isn’t only AC outlets anymore. It’s also a central charging hub for phones, tablets, drones, lights, and laptops.
 The reason it’s not the default pick is price. At $799, it’s much higher than the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 and EcoFlow DELTA 2 listings. Buy the Anker if the recharge speed and output rating are the parts you’ll use. Otherwise, spend the difference on solar, extension cords, or a second smaller station.
 Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 Portable Power Station 
 Price : $899
 Where to Buy : Amazon 
 The Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 is where portable power starts to feel like real outage planning. The useful part is 2042Wh of capacity, 2200W AC output, fast AC charging, UPS capability, a 39.5-pound weight, and a five-year manufacturer warranty.
 The reason this model matters is the weight-to-capacity ratio. Many 2kWh stations are heavy enough that you think twice before moving them. Jackery keeps this one under 40 pounds, which makes it more practical for stairs, a trunk, a garage shelf, or moving between kitchen and basement during an outage.
 This is the station I’d look at for refrigerator backup, sump pump coverage, microwave use, a remote-work setup during longer outages, or family camping where small stations start to feel like toy batteries. It has the capacity to be useful and the output to start more demanding loads.
 The warning is still load discipline. A 2kWh battery isn’t a whole-house generator. Space heaters, induction burners, hair dryers, and air conditioners can drain it fast. Use it for refrigeration, communications, lights, pumps, and short appliance bursts, and it makes sense.
 BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 Portable Power Station 
 Price : $798.99
 Where to Buy : Amazon 
 The BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 is the aggressive 2kWh value pick. The useful part is 2073.6Wh of LFP capacity, 2600W AC output, 3900W power lifting, 0 to 80 percent charging in 50 minutes, a 15ms UPS spec, and a 6000+ cycle battery claim. At $799, it undercuts several lower-output 2kWh competitors.
 This is the one I’d compare directly against the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2. The BLUETTI gives you more rated output and more listed battery-cycle headroom for less money. That’s attractive if your loads include power tools, kitchen appliances, a heavier RV setup, or longer blackout coverage.
 The trade is mass. At 53.4 pounds, the Elite 200 V2 is a luggable power station, not a casual carry. If it will live in a garage, RV, basement, or dedicated backup spot, that weight is acceptable. If it needs to move up stairs or into a trunk often, the Jackery’s lower weight becomes a real feature.
 What the specs mean in the real world
 For internet backup, the BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 is enough. A router, modem, laptop, and LED light don’t need 2kWh. Smaller also means quieter, cheaper, easier to store, and easier for someone else in the house to use.
 For camping, the BLUETTI AC70 and Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 cover the widest range. The AC70 is easier on price and still handles meaningful loads. The Jackery is the cleaner default when you want more capacity without jumping into heavy gear.
 For home outage planning, start at the BLUETTI AC180 and move up. The EcoFlow DELTA 2 is better if you want expansion and fast charging. The Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 is the lighter 2kWh station. The BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 is the high-output value play if weight isn’t the deciding factor.
 Don’t buy a portable power station because the box says “solar generator.” Buy it because the capacity, AC output, charging speed, battery chemistry, and weight match the load you plan to run.
 Final recommendation
 If I had to pick one for most readers, I’d start with the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2. It has enough capacity for useful backup, enough AC output for common loads, and a weight that still feels portable.
 If the budget is tighter, the BLUETTI AC70 is the smarter smaller step. If outage backup is the real reason you’re shopping, skip the small stuff and look at the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 or BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 instead.
 The right portable power station isn’t the biggest one you can afford. It’s the smallest one that can run the loads you truly care about.

 Introduction
 A 2,000Wh power station is the size where backup power stops being a phone charger and starts running real appliances. It holds enough energy to keep a full-size refrigerator cold for about a day, run a CPAP for several nights, or power a small RV through an evening of lights, fans and a microwave. It is also the largest size most people can still lift into a car or roll across a garage.
 The class has changed a lot in the past year. Several models that defined it, including the Anker SOLIX F2000, the original Jackery Explorer 2000 Plus and the Bluetti AC200L, have been replaced or discontinued. Newer units now add RV outlets, faster solar charging, expansion batteries and switchover times fast enough for computers.
 This guide compares the 2,000Wh models you can actually buy in the US right now. Every figure comes from the maker's own spec sheet, and we say so when a maker contradicts itself or doesn't publish a number. We left out prices because they move weekly; use the links to check the current one.

 The Best 2000Wh Portable Power Stations
 1. EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max Plus – Best Overall
 The DELTA 3 Max Plus has the most output of any 2kWh unit here, which matters when you want to run two large appliances at once, such as a well pump and a microwave, without tripping the inverter.

 Also Worth Considering

 Anker SOLIX S2000. A 2026 model built around longevity: Anker rates it at 6,000 cycles to 80% and gives it a 5-year warranty, and it weighs 35.7 lbs. The trade-off is output: 1,500W, the lowest in the class, with 400W solar. Good for long fridge or CPAP runtimes, not for power tools. See it on Amazon .
 Pecron E2400LFP. A budget 2kWh unit with 2,400W output, 3,500+ cycles to 80% and expansion to 9.7kWh, per Pecron. Its 2+1 year warranty is the shortest here. See it on Amazon .
 AFERIY P210 (Haven2400). A fixed 2,048Wh unit with 2,400W pure sine wave output, six AC outlets, 4,000+ cycles retaining over 80% and a switchover under 10 ms, per AFERIY. It can't take expansion batteries, and its 500W solar and 1,100W AC inputs are slower than the picks above, but it sits at the low end of the class. See it on Amazon · Buy direct from AFERIY (code THEPOWERSTATION for 2% off).
 Need More Than 2kWh?
 If your outage plan covers a full day of refrigeration, a well pump and a furnace blower, or you run a business from your unit, a single 2kWh battery will be tight.
 Expand a 2kWh unit. The EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max Plus, AFERIY P280, Jackery HomePower 2000 Plus v2 and DJI Power 2000 all reach 10kWh or more with extra batteries. See our expandable power station guide .
 Start bigger. The EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 holds 4,096Wh and outputs 4,000W, with 240V support for home circuits, per EcoFlow. See it on Amazon . Bluetti has also announced the Apex 200 (2,560Wh, expandable), with a US launch planned for early November.
 Our home backup guide covers whole-home setups in more detail.

 How Long Will a 2000Wh Power Station Last?
 Start with usable energy, not the label. Inverter losses mean you get roughly 85% of rated capacity out of the AC outlets, so a 2,048Wh unit delivers about 1,700Wh to AC loads. Divide that by the load in watts to get hours.

 These are estimates. Check the label or a plug-in watt meter for your own appliances, and remember that refrigerators and air conditioners cycle on and off, so their real runtime depends on the room and the weather. Our capacity guide walks through the math in more detail.
 How to Choose a 2000Wh Power Station
 Continuous output. Add up the wattage of everything you want to run at the same time and keep a margin of about 20%. A well pump or air conditioner also needs surge headroom at startup, so check the surge figure for motor loads.
 TT-30 outlet. For an RV, a TT-30R outlet lets you plug the RV's 30A cord straight in. The Anker C2000 Gen 2, AFERIY P280 and Bluetti Elite 200 V2 have one; Anker limits its outlet to 20A.
 Solar input. Higher solar input means a faster refill on a sunny day. 1,000-1,200W can refill a 2kWh battery in about 2-3 hours of strong sun; 800W takes closer to 3-4 hours.
 Expansion. If you might need more than 2kWh later, choose a unit with an expansion battery now. Expansion packs are usually tied to one model or family, so you can't mix brands.
 UPS switchover. For computers, networking gear and medical devices, look for 10 ms or less. Bluetti's 15 ms and EcoFlow DELTA 2 Max's unstated figure are fine for most appliances.
 Weight. Every unit here is 41-54 lbs. If you'll carry it often, the Anker C2000 Gen 2 and Jackery HomePower 2000 Plus v2 are the lightest.
 Warranty and cycle rating. Read the fine print: some warranty years require registration or buying from the maker's store, and cycle ratings use different end points (70% or 80%).
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Can a 2000Wh power station replace a home generator?
 For selected circuits, yes. A 2kWh unit can keep a refrigerator, lights, Wi-Fi, phones and a CPAP running through a typical overnight outage. It can't run central air conditioning, an electric range or a water heater, and it will need recharging (solar, wall power or a generator) to cover multi-day outages. Many households pair a power station for quiet, automatic backup with a generator they run a few hours a day to recharge it. Our power stations vs generators guide compares the two.
 How long until the battery degrades?
 Every unit on this list uses LiFePO4 cells rated for 3,000-6,000 cycles. A cycle is one full discharge; using half the battery counts as half a cycle. At one partial cycle a day, that is many years before the battery reaches its rated end point (70% or 80% of original capacity, depending on the maker). A battery at 80% still works; it just holds less. Lithium cells also age with time, so store the unit at about 50-60% charge when you won't use it for a while, and top it up every few months.
 Can I connect solar panels from a different brand?
 Usually yes, as long as you stay within the power station's input limits. Check two numbers: the maximum input voltage and the maximum input wattage. Measure or calculate your array's open-circuit voltage (panels in series add their voltages) and make sure it stays below the limit, for example 60V on the Jackery HomePower 2000 Plus v2 and the Bluetti Elite 200 V2, or 55V on the AFERIY P280. You may also need an adapter from MC4 to the station's port (XT60, XT90 or Anderson).
 Can I run a 30A RV on a 2000Wh power station?
 You can plug in through a TT-30 outlet, but the power station limits what you can run. At 2,400-2,800W you can run lights, the fridge, the water pump and a microwave in turn, but not the roof air conditioner and the microwave together. A 13,500 BTU RV air conditioner draws well over 1,000W while its compressor runs, so it would drain a 2kWh battery in little more than an hour of compressor time.
 Is 2000Wh enough for a CPAP?
 Yes, with plenty of margin. A CPAP without a heated humidifier draws about 40-60W, so a 2kWh unit covers several nights. Turning off the humidifier and running the CPAP from a DC cable, where the maker offers one, stretches it further. See our CPAP power station guide .
 Conclusion
 For most buyers, the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max Plus is the most capable 2kWh unit you can buy right now, with the highest output and a 10kWh expansion path. RV owners should look at the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 for its TT-30 outlet and alternator charging, or the AFERIY P280 for more output, more solar input and a longer warranty at a lower price. If you want one box with nothing to add, the Bluetti Elite 200 V2 has the best like-for-like cycle rating and a TT-30 outlet.
 Whatever you choose, size it to your real loads first: list what must run during an outage, total the watts and the hours, and leave a margin.
